name: Elena Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the South Park station, and I split my week between response shifts and being the school liaison officer for two secondary schools. At the schools I run talks on knife crime and online safety, and I deal with fights, phone thefts, the occasional kid carrying something they shouldn't. On response it's the usual: shoplifting, car crashes, a missing teenager. I love the school days, because you can stop something before it starts. The thing that wears me out is the rota, which changes every month.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé Arjun, and we're saving for a house. Arjun runs his family's hardware shop on Station Road, which his grandfather opened. The shop's been struggling for a few years because people buy everything online now. We help at the temple on Sundays, and my parents live ten minutes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things are always oversold. At work I'd keep using the scheduling tool I already use now and then. I'd tell my school kids that the tools are useful but they still need to learn properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, my job is secure and the pay is good. The worry in our house is the shop, not AI. Arjun's takings are down about a fifth on three years ago, and that's with or without clever computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and try for a permanent school liaison role. We'd keep putting money aside for the house, we've got more than six months of my pay saved. And I'd help Arjun set up a better website for the shop on my days off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, but uneasy about the shop. It's on my mind most weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the shop.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My fiancé Arjun's grandfather opened the shop in 1979, and now the big online sellers do the same screws and paint for less, delivered next day. The whole family has worked there. Arjun works six days a week and still worries about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the shop closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be all right because of my pay, but it would break Arjun's heart and his dad's. The family would expect him to find something else fast. We'd probably push the wedding back a bit.

say: AI was **oversold**, as these things usually are.
Pupils still need to **learn properly**, even with useful tools.
think: Her **job is secure**, but the family **shop** is the household worry.
Takings at Arjun's (her fiancé's) shop are **down a fifth**.
do: Apply for a **permanent school liaison** role.
Keep saving for **the house** with over six months saved.
Build the **shop website** on her days off.
feel: **Mostly fine**, but **uneasy** about the shop most weeks.

fieldNote: Her household pressure is the **struggling family shop**, not AI.
Her own job is **secure**, which carries the household.
She'd **help the shop** with her own time, a family-first instinct.

steps.text: Apply for a permanent school liaison role
Keep saving for the house deposit
Build a better website for Arjun's hardware shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we should take it seriously, but not lose our heads. At work I'd say it could free us up to do more face-to-face work in the schools. I'd tell the parents' evening crowd to watch what their kids are using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is fine, maybe even better. The schools work is all about trust, and nobody can send software to sit with a fourteen-year-old who's being groomed online. The bigger worry is Arjun, because AI makes online shopping even cheaper and smarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new AI tools once a few colleagues have tried them, probably in the first six months. I'd sit down with Arjun and his dad and help them use AI for stock ordering and the website. And we'd keep the wedding for next summer, but look at a cheaper venue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I feel safe for me, worried for Arjun's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI makes online shopping smarter. What does that mean for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big sites will know what you need before you do, and send it the same day. Arjun's only advantage is advice, knowing which fitting goes with which pipe. Maybe that's enough for older customers, but not for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the shop went under?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the computers, really. Big firms that don't pay their fair share of tax, and councils that put the rents up on Station Road. Small family shops are the backbone of a street, and nobody protects them.

say: AI is a big change to take seriously, but we shouldn't **lose our heads**.
AI could free officers for more **face-to-face** school work.
think: School liaison runs on **trust**, which software can't replace.
The **real risk** is to Arjun's (her fiancé's) shop from smarter online selling.
do: Learn the **AI tools** once colleagues have tried them.
Help the family use AI for **stock ordering**.
Keep the **wedding date** but find a cheaper venue.
feel: **Safe** for herself and **worried** for Arjun's family.
S1.quote: Nobody can send software to sit with a fourteen-year-old who's being groomed online.
fieldNote: She sees her **school work** as protected by trust.
She blames **big firms and rents**, not the technology.
Her plans are **family plans**: shop, wedding, house.

steps.text: Learn the force's AI tools once colleagues have tested them
Help Arjun and his dad use AI for stock ordering
Book a cheaper venue for next summer's wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after each other, families and communities, because the government won't be ready. At work I'd say the police still need people the public trust. At the temple I'd probably help organise something for people who lose their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's frightening. The thinking side of policing, the reports, the checks, the intelligence, goes in 2028. My school work is mostly people work, so maybe I'd last until the robots in 2031, maybe longer. But the shop would be gone, I think, and then we'd be one income in a world that's falling apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house search straight away and keep everything in savings. We'd still get married, but small, at the temple, family only. I'd move to the school liaison role full time, because that's the part of the job that's most about people. And I'd talk to my parents about all of us pooling money if things get hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying a lot. I'd feel like I have to hold everyone together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one income. Is that a real fear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If the shop closes, my fiancé Arjun is 29 with a family business and no other qualifications. Mine would be the only steady pay for us, and maybe for his parents too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the kids in the schools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to stay curious and stay kind, because those are the things that last. And I'd tell them to look after their families. That's what my parents told me.

say: Families and communities must **look after each other**, because the government won't be ready.
Police still need **people the public trust**.
think: Her **school work** might last until 2031, but the shop would likely close.
She fears becoming the **only income** for the wider family.
do: Stop the **house search** and keep everything saved.
Hold a **small temple wedding**, family only.
Talk to her parents about **pooling money**.
feel: She feels she must **hold everyone together**.
S2.quote: If the shop closes, my fiancé Arjun is 29 with a family business and no other qualifications.
fieldNote: Her **own job** feels safer than the household's.
She turns to **faith and family** rather than government.
She'd **shrink the wedding** but never cancel it.

steps.text: Stop the house search and keep the deposit in savings
Hold a small family wedding at the temple
Agree with her parents to pool money if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if families plan together. At work I'd push for the force to keep school officers and train everyone on the new systems early. At the temple I'd suggest a group for people wanting to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still a big worry, mostly for the shop and for Arjun. I'd be 32 when AGI arrives and 35 when the robots do. My job would probably shrink, but the people part might survive. The shop has five years to find a new way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Arjun turn the shop into something more like a repair and fitting service, because you can't do that from a website. I'd do the force's AI course in the first year. We'd buy a smaller house with a bigger deposit. And I'd keep a year's pay in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, less sharply. It's more planning than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A repair and fitting service. Has Arjun ever done that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not officially, but customers ask him all the time. My fiancé Arjun has fitted taps for half the street for free. If he charged for it, it might keep the doors open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when the robots arrive in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then maybe the robots fit the taps too, I don't know. By then I hope we've got the house paid down and a bit put by. I can't plan for everything.

say: Five years is enough if **families plan together**.
The force should **keep school officers** and train everyone early.
think: Her **job may shrink**, but the people part may survive.
Arjun's (her fiancé's) **shop** has five years to find a new way.
do: Help turn the shop into a **repair and fitting** service.
Do the force's **AI course** in year one.
Buy a **smaller house** with a bigger deposit.
S3.quote: My fiancé Arjun has fitted taps for half the street for free.
fieldNote: She looks for the **hands-on service** the shop can sell.

steps.text: Help Arjun start a paid repair and fitting service
Do the force's AI course in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good long time, so people should use it well. At work I'd say let's get the training right. At home I'd say the same to Arjun's dad: plan now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm uneasy but not scared. I'd be 37 and 40 when it all lands, with a house and, I hope, children. The shop might change completely by then, and so might my job, but we'd have time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married next summer as planned and buy a house the year after. I'd learn the AI tools as they come into the force. I'd help Arjun build the repair side of the shop slowly. And I'd keep saving, because that's what my parents taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. It's there, but it's not running my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still have children on your timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, ten years is enough. I'd want them to grow up with grandparents nearby and a mum with a steady job. I think we'd manage that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing you'd most want to protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family, always. The job matters, the shop matters, but the family is what gets you through anything.

say: Ten years is **a good long time** to use well.
She'd tell Arjun's dad to **plan now**, not later.
think: At **37 and 40** she'd hope to have a house and children.
Both the **shop and her job** may change, but there's time.
do: Marry **next summer** and buy a house the year after.
Build the **repair side** of the shop slowly.
Keep **saving steadily** as her parents taught.
feel: **Quietly uneasy**, but it's not running her **life**.
S4.quote: The job matters, the shop matters, but the family is what gets you through anything.
fieldNote: With ten years, her **family plans go ahead** unchanged.
**Family** is her answer to every scenario.
The shop's **slow decline** stays a background worry, even with a decade to adjust.

steps.text: Marry next summer and buy a house the year after
Learn the force's AI tools as they arrive

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit the shop and the police at the same time, and I'd be holding the whole family together. What would help is the force keeping school and community officers, and some help for small family businesses to change what they sell, like cheap loans or training, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids I work with. They're growing up with all this, and they're scared too. Somebody needs to talk to them honestly.

headlineQuote: Small family shops are the backbone of a street, and nobody protects them.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old officer** at South Park who splits her week between response and **school liaison**.
Her own job feels **secure**, but her fiancé Arjun's family **hardware shop** is already struggling.
She blames **big firms and rents** rather than technology, and turns to family and faith.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious** about being the only income; ten years lets plans go ahead.
Every plan comes back to **family**: the shop, a small wedding, a house and children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hitting the **shop** and the police at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping **school and community officers** in the force.
**Cheap loans or training** for small family businesses, not handouts.
